claims.text: The identity of X is the primary factor governing formation and persistence of a coherent protective oxide scale in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
Al additions promote formation of a slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 scale.
Si additions promote formation of a slow-growing, adherent SiO2 scale.
Mn additions form faster-growing, volatile manganese oxides.
Manganese oxides cannot accommodate internal growth stresses and consequently crack and spall.
Controlled metal and oxygen diffusion at the surface enables protective Al2O3 or SiO2 scale formation.
Al and Si have strong oxygen affinities.
Compact Al- and Si-rich oxide scales reduce further oxygen ingress.
Compact Al- and Si-rich oxide scales relieve internal stresses.
Mn oxidizes more rapidly than Al or Si in the proposed alloy comparison.
Rapid Mn oxidation produces less-stable oxides with high internal stresses.
Al-containing alloys will show less spallation and mass loss than Mn-containing and baseline CrFeCoNi alloys under identical tests.
Si-containing alloys will show less spallation and mass loss than Mn-containing and baseline CrFeCoNi alloys under identical tests.
Mn-containing and baseline CrFeCoNi alloys will develop unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide layers.
The absence of Al or Si results in less-stable oxide coverage.
The proposed behavior applies to single- or multiphase solid-solution alloys containing no more than approximately 10 at.% X.
The proposed behavior applies above 900 °C at oxygen partial pressures similar to those in 1 atm air.
Multiphase microstructures may modify oxidation behavior.
A lack of statistically significant improvement for Al- and Si-containing alloys, or formation of a similarly protective scale by Mn-containing alloys, would falsify the hypothesis.
